newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton brands his mark on APEC.
newsitem.headline: Clinton brands his mark on APEC.

text.p: In his first foreign foray since winning re-election, President Bill Clinton made the fourth APEC summit his own.

He broke 10 years of ice with China and wrestled a key trade concession from fellow world leaders when the U.S. cause seemed to have been lost by his experts in the Commerce, Trade and State departments.

"It's amazing," said an awed aide who took part in many of the formal and informal talks held by Clinton at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which ended with a one-day summit at Subic Bay north of Manila on Monday.
"It was different in the beginning... ," the aide said, contrasting Clinton's easy mastery of a major world forum with his tentative tiptoeing out of Arkansas onto the world stage four years ago.
The breakthrough with China grabbed all the headlines as leaders of 18 economies representing half the world's people and international business were gathering in Manila at the weekend.
In a move that put him alongside U.S.-China movers such as Richard Nixon and George Bush, Clinton agreed on Sunday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin to exchange summits in each other's capital.
The Sino-U.S. relationship had been frosty for almost a decade since the Beijing authorities cruelly crushed democratic dissent in Tiananmen Square.
Only last March, Clinton sent two battle fleets to Taiwan to bolster what China regards as a renegade province in the face of missile threats.

Human rights, arms proliferation, intellectual property rights and market opening have all bedevilled relations between the existing superpower and the one that many believe will dominate the 21st century.
The smiling handshake between Clinton and Jiang cast a warm glow over the summit and beyond. Many Asians hailed it as a sunny omen for the "Pacific Century".
"It is a marked improvement over the low-point in Sino-American relations..." said Geremie Barme, a China scholar.
"For the Chinese to have engaged positively with the Americans in this type of public meeting between presidents is significant."

Before Clinton flew into Manila, the omens were not good for the deal the United States wanted on global trade in computers and telecommunications equipment, seen by many as the building blocks for the 21st century.

Two days of wrangling in APEC ministerial sessions by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor failed to secure anything more than a panacea to shuffle the issue on to the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore next month.
Clinton, his power and prestige immensely enhanced by his sweeping re-election victory in the November 5 presidential election, went to work on key leaders.

In private talks with Jiang, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, South Korean President Kim Young-sam, Philippine President Fidel Ramos and others, he pressed relentlessly his view that APEC had to move positively towards dropping tariffs on a business worth at least $500 billion a year.
The United States sells $100 billion worth of information technology every year and almost two million jobs depend on the business.
After a sales job by the president, the other leaders finally agreed to put some "oomph" -- the White House's word -- into the issue left limp by the ministers.
The summit declaration called on WTO to conclude an agreement to substantially reduce tariffs by the year 2000.
"We are absolutely delighted..." said U.S.-APEC coordinator John Wolf.
Clinton, looking extremely satisfied, told embassy staff afterwards simply that it was "a big deal."
